candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns 0.97 probability of malware, and all 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking. The supplied evidence itself is thin. The top-20 SHAP contributions are small and evenly spread, from +0.0050 to +0.0127, and sum to about +0.132. No single feature dominates. Fourteen of the 20 n-grams have a displayed relative frequency of 0.000000, so they are rare or absent in the binary. The six with non-zero frequencies are all very low (sub strb 0.000887, eor strb 0.000551, orr bic 0.000173, eor sub 0.000072, mvn orr 0.000020, and b 0.000002). No function names or locations were provided, so none of these patterns can be tied to a specific routine such as a hashing loop. The n-grams are generic. Some are bitwise or arithmetic mixing patterns (XOR XOR, XOR SHL, XOR CMOVNZ, eor sub, eor strb, orr bic, mvn orr), which can be consistent with hash or cipher-style computation. Others are ordinary control-flow and call glue (TEST JZ, CMP JL, MOV JZ, LEA CALL, CALL ADD, ADD POP, SUB LEA) that appears in almost any compiled code. The set also mixes uppercase x86-style mnemonics and lowercase ARM-style mnemonics, which the evidence does not explain. The model's score is high, but the n-gram evidence does not independently show mining behavior such as a compute-intensive loop or mining-related routines. The case is therefore suggestive but inconclusive.
